rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient that spans the full organic range at moderate temperature to reveal the elution window, detect any unretained or missing late compounds, and give a baseline for how much retention shortening temperature provides.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the objective is to pull the last peak under 10 minutes without losing resolution. The first run suggests the useful elution window is only about phi 0.10 to 0.44, so a shorter, narrower gradient with higher temperature should keep all peaks in-gradient while reducing overall retention.

The only problem is the 6/7 pair, and it collapsed when the gradient was made steeper, so the next step is to keep the successful retention window and temperature but make the gradient shallower. This should selectively recover resolution for that slope-sensitive pair while likely keeping the last peak under 10 minutes.

Changing tG in the same window made the critical pair worse, so that pair is not helped by slope here and likely needs a selectivity shift instead. Drop back to the faster 10 min gradient that kept t_last under 10 min, but lower temperature to test whether the 6/7 pair separates better at cooler conditions while staying near the time target.

The critical 6/7 pair improved strongly when temperature was lowered, while timing is still comfortably under 10 minutes at 40 C. A slightly cooler run with a modestly narrower upper phi should further shift selectivity around the crowded mid-gradient region without much risk of pushing the last peak past 10 minutes.

Lowering temperature helped one critical region but narrowing the upper window too far created a new 5/6 compression and pushed the last peak just past 10 minutes. Keep the cooler temperature that improved selectivity, but widen the window slightly upward to relieve mid-late crowding and recover some speed.

The best run so far is at 40 C, while moving to 35 C over-compressed a different pair; this suggests the optimum selectivity is likely between 40 and 50 C. Test 45 C with the same successful gradient window and duration to see if the critical pair can be nudged above 1.17 without sacrificing the sub-10-minute last peak.

Temperature studies show 40 C is best for the critical selectivity, so keep T at 40 and fine-tune the gradient shape instead. A slightly longer and slightly broader gradient may open the crowded middle region enough to lift the worst pair above 1.5 while likely keeping the last peak near 10 minutes.

Injection 8 is very close: only a tiny shortfall in the 6/7 pair and a 0.2 min time penalty. Since 40 C gave the best selectivity family and lower temperature previously shifted which pair was critical, testing 35 C at this improved gradient shape may push the near-critical pair over 1.5 with only a small risk of extra retention.

The best method is extremely close, with only a slight time penalty and the 6/7 pair just under full credit. Increase phi1 one step while keeping the successful tG and temperature, aiming to pull the last peak under 10 minutes with minimal disturbance to the selectivity pattern.

Raising phi1 fixed the time penalty but hurt the critical 6/7 resolution, so the best shape remains the 0.75/12 min gradient. Test 45 C on that shape to see whether a modest temperature shift can pull the last peak under 10 minutes while preserving the near-baseline separation better than the broader window did.

The 0.75/12 min/40 C method is nearly optimal, and the critical pair appears to benefit from the 40 C selectivity and this phi window. Make the gradient just one step shallower to try to push the 6/7 pair clearly above 1.5; although t_last may rise slightly, the gain in resolution could still improve CRF.

The 14 min gradient fully resolves everything, but the time penalty is too large; compared with the 12 min run, the critical pair clearly benefits from shallower slope. Raise phi1 one step while keeping tG 14 and T 40 to retain full resolution but compress the late part enough to try to bring t_last closer to 10 minutes.

The first peak is not close to unretained, so raising phi0 one step should trim dead low-organic time and may slightly compress the early region without strongly affecting the critical mid-gradient pair. This is a small local perturbation around the best method that could shave the last-peak time penalty while preserving selectivity.

You already reached the maximum CRF, so this run should probe how robust the optimum is while staying close to the winning conditions. Raising phi0 one more step tests whether additional trimming of the unused low-organic region preserves full resolution and keeps the last peak under 10 minutes.

The method remains at the CRF maximum after increasing phi0 to 0.15, and the first peak is still retained, so one more upward step tests how far the low end can be trimmed while preserving full credit. This explores whether the optimum can be made more aggressive without collapsing the critical mid-pack pair.

The optimum is robust at phi0 0.10-0.15, but pushing phi0 to 0.20 starts to erode the critical pair. With phi0 fixed at the best faster setting of 0.15, lower phi1 one step to see whether a slightly narrower window restores extra margin on the 6/7 pair while keeping t_last below 10 minutes.

At phi0 0.15, lowering phi1 improved resolution margin but pushed the last peak just over 10 minutes, so the opposite direction should test the speed edge of the optimum. This checks whether a slightly broader upper window can keep full credit while shortening the run further.

Both CRF-1.000 methods sit on a good plateau, and the tradeoff around them is now clear: higher phi1 gains speed but weakens the critical pair, while lower phi0 appears to strengthen that pair. Testing phi0 0.10 with phi1 0.80 probes whether that combination can keep full resolution while retaining the shorter last-peak time.

You already have CRF 1.000, so the remaining value is mapping the speed/resolution boundary near the optimum. Shortening tG from 12 to 10 min at the proven phi window will test whether the method can be made faster while still keeping all adjacent pairs at or above 1.5.

The 10 min gradient became too steep at phi0 0.15, so lower phi0 to 0.10 to strengthen the critical 6/7 pair while keeping the same fast run time regime. This tests whether the winning lower-start composition can preserve full resolution even at the shorter gradient length.

The 12 min optimum is established, so the remaining information gain is about robustness on either side of that point at the better phi0 of 0.15. A 14 min run here should show whether the extra low-end trimming maintains the full-resolution margin seen at longer gradient time, even though CRF itself is unlikely to improve.

Both phi0 0.10 and 0.15 with phi1 0.75 are optimal, and lowering phi1 at phi0 0.15 improved resolution but slightly missed the 10-minute limit. Testing the analogous lower phi1 at phi0 0.10 checks whether the lower start can recover just enough speed-resolution balance to stay at full credit.

With the optimum already achieved, the only unexplored local degree of freedom around the winning shape is temperature at phi0 0.10. A cooler run tests robustness of the CRF-1.000 method to temperature and confirms whether the excellent selectivity at 40 C is truly a sharp optimum.

A final nearby check around the winning conditions is to pair the successful lower phi0 with a slightly shallower gradient, which should preserve full resolution and maps robustness on the slow side of the optimum. It is unlikely to beat CRF 1.000, but it is the most informative untested neighbor of the best method.
